**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 63, verses 9–11:**

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, it is those who are the losers.﴾ ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

*Al-ilha'* (diversion, distraction) means being occupied with desire and pleasure. "The remembrance of Allah" here is general: it includes monotheism, prayer, supplication, and other obligatory and recommended acts. This is the view of al-Hasan and a group of exegetes. Al-Dahhak, 'Ata' and his companions said that the intended "remembrance" is the prescribed prayer. The first view is more apparent. Similarly, the words of the Exalted, ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾, were said by most of those who interpreted it to mean zakat. Others said it is general, covering both obligatory and recommended charity. The words ﴿before death comes to one of you﴾ mean its signs and its first beginnings. The words ﴿if only You would delay me for a brief term﴾ are a request for a return and a respite. In the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads *"akhkhartan"* without the *ya'* (the first-person suffix *-ni*). He called it "brief" because it is coming. Moreover, one only wishes for that in order to perform righteous deeds in the time, and at that point hope does not extend to seeking livelihood and managing it. In the codex of Ubayy it reads *"fa-atasaddaq"* (with the *ta'* assimilated into the sad, as a variant reading of *fa-asaddaq*). The words of the Exalted, ﴿and be among the righteous﴾, apparently have a general meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said that it means Hajj. It is related from him that he said one day in his assembly: "There is no man who does not pay zakat and perform Hajj except that he seeks a return at his death." A man said to him, "Do you not fear Allah? Does a believer seek a return?" Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to him, "Yes," and then recited the verse.

Most of the Seven Readers and the people read *"wa-akun"* with *jazm* (the apocopated form), as a conjunction joining it to the place (*mahall*) of the preceding verb, because the sense is: "If You delay me, I will give charity and be among the righteous." This is the position of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for what Sibawayh related from al-Khalil, it is different from this: the verb is put in the jussive on the assumption of a conditional (*shart*) that is implied by the wish. There is no *mahall* here, because the conditional is not explicit. A verb is conjoined to the place only where the conditional clearly appears, as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them﴾ [al-A'raf: 186]. Whoever reads with *jazm* conjoins to the place of *"fa-la hadiya lahu"* (there is no guide for him), because there a verb occurred that was in the jussive. Likewise, whoever reads *"wa-yakfur"* in the jussive conjoins it to the place of *(fa-huwa khayrun lakum)* (it is better for you). Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Abi Ishaq, Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-'Anbari read *"wa-akun"* in the accusative (*nasb*), conjoining it to *"fa-asaddaq."* Abu Hatim said, regarding its writing in the codex without a *waw*, that they omitted the *waw* just as they omitted it from *"ittakhadha"* and others. Abu 'Ali preferred this reading. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, it reads *"fa-atasaddaq wa-akun."*

The words of the Exalted, ﴿But Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come﴾, contain an exhortation to hasten and to race against the term with righteous deeds. The Seven Readers and most people read *"ta'malun"* (you do) with the *ta'*, addressing all people. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read *"ya'malun"* (they do) with the *ya'*, restricting the warning to the disbelievers.

The commentary on Surat al-Munafiqun is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Similarly, the words of the Exalted, ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾, were said by most of those who interpreted it to mean zakat. Others said it is general, covering both obligatory and recommended charity. The words ﴿before death comes to one of you﴾ mean its signs and its first beginnings. The words ﴿if only You would delay me for a brief term﴾ are a request for a return and a respite. In the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads *"akhkhartan"* without the *ya'* (the first-person suffix *-ni*). He called it "brief" because it is coming. Moreover, one only wishes for that in order to perform righteous deeds in the time, and at that point hope does not extend to seeking livelihood and managing it. In the codex of Ubayy it reads *"fa-atasaddaq"* (with the *ta'* assimilated into the sad, as a variant reading of *fa-asaddaq*). The words of the Exalted, ﴿and be among the righteous﴾, apparently have a general meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said that it means Hajj. It is related from him that he said one day in his assembly: "There is no man who does not pay zakat and perform Hajj except that he seeks a return at his death." A man said to him, "Do you not fear Allah? Does a believer seek a return?" Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said to him, "Yes," and then recited the verse.

Most of the Seven Readers and the people read *"wa-akun"* with *jazm* (the apocopated form), as a conjunction joining it to the place (*mahall*) of the preceding verb, because the sense is: "If You delay me, I will give charity and be among the righteous." This is the position of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for what Sibawayh related from al-Khalil, it is different from this: the verb is put in the jussive on the assumption of a conditional (*shart*) that is implied by the wish. There is no *mahall* here, because the conditional is not explicit. A verb is conjoined to the place only where the conditional clearly appears, as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them﴾ [al-A'raf: 186]. Whoever reads with *jazm* conjoins to the place of *"fa-la hadiya lahu"* (there is no guide for him), because there a verb occurred that was in the jussive. Likewise, whoever reads *"wa-yakfur"* in the jussive conjoins it to the place of *(fa-huwa khayrun lakum)* (it is better for you). Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Abi Ishaq, Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-'Anbari read *"wa-akun"* in the accusative (*nasb*), conjoining it to *"fa-asaddaq."* Abu Hatim said, regarding its writing in the codex without a *waw*, that they omitted the *waw* just as they omitted it from *"ittakhadha"* and others. Abu 'Ali preferred this reading. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them, it reads *"fa-atasaddaq wa-akun."*

The words of the Exalted, ﴿But Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come﴾, contain an exhortation to hasten and to race against the term with righteous deeds. The Seven Readers and most people read *"ta'malun"* (you do) with the *ta'*, addressing all people. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read *"ya'malun"* (they do) with the *ya'*, restricting the warning to the disbelievers.

The commentary on Surat al-Munafiqun is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
